verdict: Avoid new specialty & fine chemicals exposure in Bharuch for now; lend only to established, compliance-clean, multi-customer units with tight working-capital control, and decline single-plant or trading-heavy proposals.
title: Bharuch specialty & fine chemicals: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A specialty/fine chemicals unit in Bharuch buys basic feedstock (chlor-alkali, amines, solvents), runs multi-step batch or continuous reactions, and sells small volumes of high-value molecules to pharma, agro and fuel-additive buyers.** Cash turns on conversion yield, plant uptime and the ability to pass input costs through; value sits in the customer qualification, not the reactor. **The working-capital cycle is the real risk: inventory and receivables block capital, and ICRA flags elevated working-capital intensity that worsens in high-growth phases [8][9].** So when a proposal lands, check the receivable days and inventory holding against peers before you look at the P&L.

## What has changed now
**The macro backdrop is against us: IIP for NIC 20 chemicals is -0.5% YoY and -1.2% Apr-to-date, while bank credit to industry is running +20.7% YoY — a +21.9 pp gap that says lending is outrunning output [D].** Brent at $113/bbl sits above the $75–100 band [D], squeezing feedstock and freight. **Locally, GPCB ordered immediate closure of Aarti Drugs' Bharuch amines plant in July 2026 for environmental non-compliance, with revenue impact and timeline unresolved [3].** That is the single most important local fact: compliance failure can stop cash flow overnight. **Peer results are strong but not local — Aarti Industries posted Q2 FY27 PAT up 60% to ₹169 crore on 30% volume growth [6], and revenue up 75% to ₹3,668 crore [4]; treat these as peer benchmarks, not Bharuch evidence.** Sources say little specific about Bharuch borrower-level performance, so lean on first principles and these peers.

## Where the growth is
**Pursue established units with diversified end-use customers (pharma, agro, fuel additives) and a track record of cost pass-through, as ICRA notes pass-through mitigates raw-material and forex risk [8].** DCM Shriram is expanding chloride capacity at Bharuch [2], so ancillary and feedstock-linked suppliers to that chain are natural prospects. **Avoid single-plant, single-customer units, trading-heavy firms whose debt is all working capital [11], and any borrower with a live or recent GPCB notice.**

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the working-capital cycle: cash-flow-based limits, monthly stock-and-receivable statements, and a covenant capping inventory plus receivables days.** Take monthly GPCB consent status, effluent data and insurance on stock. **Because capex stays elevated in this sector [9], require promoter contribution and a term-debt cap; do not fund expansion on receivables.**

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for stretched receivable days, rising inventory, any GPCB direction, and feedstock cost not being passed through.** If a borrower's receivable days climb month-on-month, cut limits and ask for the customer-wise ageing.
watch: any notice or closure -> freeze limits and reassess
rising trend -> cut limit, demand ageing
build-up without orders -> require stock statement and reduce drawing power
falling yield -> ask for maintenance capex plan
